hook.line: Tomás has been waiting for Vale all morning and she has not called. In English you would say "that's odd". Spanish says it with a frame that always pulls the next verb into the subjunctive.
hook.es: Me extraña que Vale no haya llamado.
hook.en: It's odd that Vale hasn't called.

examples.es: Me extraña que no haya llamado.
examples.en: It's odd that he hasn't called.
How strange that she isn't answering!

examples.es: Me llama la atención que nadie diga nada.
examples.en: I find it striking that nobody says anything.

examples.es: Me extraña que Vale no haya venido.
examples.en: It's odd that Vale hasn't come.

examples.es: Me extraña que la tienda esté cerrada.
examples.en: It's odd that the shop is closed.

rule:
To react with surprise, use *me extraña que*, *me sorprende que*, *me llama la atención que* or *¡Qué raro que...!*

The next verb goes in the subjunctive, even though the fact is true:
*estás* becomes *estés*, *contesta* becomes *conteste*, *ha llamado* becomes *haya llamado*.

English keeps the plain verb ("I'm surprised you're here"). Spanish changes it. The surprise works like *gustar*: the odd thing is what causes it and you are *me*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the subjunctive of emotional reaction. It is used even when the fact is not in doubt.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *estás* or *estés* and type the whole sentence: *Me sorprende que ___ aquí.* (I'm surprised you're here.)
yourTurn.why: After *me sorprende que*, the verb goes into the subjunctive: *estés*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *ha llamado* or *haya llamado* and type the whole sentence: *Me extraña que no ___.* (It's odd that he hasn't called.)
yourTurn.answer: Me extraña que no haya llamado.
yourTurn.why: *Haya* is the subjunctive helper for "hasn't done".

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: How strange that she isn't answering!
yourTurn.why: *¡Qué raro que...!* also takes the subjunctive: *conteste*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I find it striking that nobody says anything.
yourTurn.answer: Me llama la atención que nadie diga nada.
yourTurn.why: *Me llama la atención que* is another surprise frame, so *diga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It's odd that Vale hasn't come.
yourTurn.answer: Me extraña que Vale no haya venido.
yourTurn.why: *Me extraña que* + the perfect subjunctive for something that has not happened.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it about Hernando: *Me extraña que Vale no haya venido.* (It's odd that Hernando hasn't come.)
yourTurn.answer: Me extraña que Hernando no haya venido.
yourTurn.why: Only the name changes; *haya* is the same for he, she and you (formal).

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: I'm surprised you've come back.

pitfalls.wrong: Me extraña que no ha llamado.
pitfalls.right: Me extraña que no haya llamado.
pitfalls.why: Almost. A reaction to a fact still takes the subjunctive, so *ha* becomes *haya*.
Almost. English keeps "you're", but Spanish switches to *estés*.

pitfalls.right: Me extraña que no haya llamado.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Extraño* alone means "I miss"; to be surprised you need *me extraña*.

personal: Think of something that surprised you this week and say it with *Me extraña que...* or *Me sorprende que...*.
